properties.name: Flying with Ember

properties.description: The drake she raises. Solving math earns the hoard — copper, silver, gold, crowns, trading ten-for-one — and the hoard feeds Ember, builds its nest, then its cave. The reason to come back tomorrow is Ember, not a score. Per dec:built-for-understanding the hoard must be earned by reasoning, never by speed or lucky guesses: what earning looks like concretely is still open, and it is the same question as how we would know she understood something.
properties.name: Raising Ember

properties.description: The opening gate. Takes her back through 3rd grade math — multiplication and division within 100, fractions as numbers, area and perimeter, time and data, shapes — and Grade 4 does not open until she clears it. How long it is and what "cleared" means are still open, and dec:grade3-is-a-gate records the risk that a gate she cannot clear is a game she stops playing.
properties.name: Grade 3 gate

properties.description: Carries the player through the five Grade 4 NYS domains — OA, NBT, NF, MD, G — as playable content rather than chapters.
properties.name: Grade 4 play-through

properties.description: When she finishes Grade 4, the game keeps going into Grade 5 instead of ending: decimals and the place value system, unlike denominators, multiplying and dividing fractions, volume, the coordinate plane. Open-ended — she reaches it by getting there, and nothing requires her to.
properties.name: Climb into Grade 5

properties.description: Feeding Ember and taking Ember for walks, between lessons. Feeding is already described under Raising Ember as something the earned hoard pays for; walks are new. What a walk IS — time with Ember, or a place the mathematics turns up (distance, time, the route) — is not decided, and neither is whether looking after Ember moves her along at all. Whatever it becomes, it must not be a second road to Ember's growth that skips the teaching: the owner has told the player that flying comes from the lessons.
properties.name: Looking after Ember

properties.description: Every screen holds one mathematical idea, sized for a phone held in one hand in portrait, driven by taps and single-finger drags. No hover, no typing, no pinch-zoom to read a diagram.

NOT CONFIRMED: whether the owner wants any way to see how she is doing, and what happens if she clears her browser data or switches phones.

properties.description: A problem at the end of the grade that Ember works through unaided while the player watches — laying it out, counting it the fast way, turning it, walling it, breaking the hard number apart — naming the lesson she is reaching for each time. The player's part is to have taught her already.
properties.name: The quest Ember takes alone

properties.description: Interactive visual models that carry the explanation: arrays and area models for multiplication, fraction bars and number lines for equivalence, a draggable protractor for angles, shapes you can sort by their properties.
properties.name: Pictures you can touch
Styling only for the name field and the recall chip — no design meaning beyond the two features already recorded.
properties.subject: system

properties.name: Every asset cache-busted, and the build number made visible
properties.rationale: A fix that was correct on disk, correctly deployed and correctly reported was still not what the owner's browser served: it held the previous main.js. GitHub Pages sets its own cache headers and this project cannot change them, so the URL is the only thing able to tell a browser that a file moved. This matters past the incident — she will open a bookmark every time, and a stale copy is the one failure a nine-year-old could not describe.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary: Assets are loaded with a ?v=N stamp sharing one build number, a favicon was inlined as a data URI to remove the page's only failing request, and the build number is logged at boot so a stale copy can be identified rather than guessed at.

properties.name: Ember becomes a girl, everywhere the game, the README and the design say so
properties.rationale: Owner's word, 2026-09-30 (dec:ember-is-a-girl). The stamp has to move with any asset change or a phone that already loaded build 3 keeps showing "him" — the trap recorded in the verify-the-path rule.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary: Every he/him/his for Ember becomes she/her: on screen (the door line, "Go and meet her", "Tell her", "See what she can do", "Watch her do it again", "She has a nest.", "She did it without you.", the page and share descriptions), in code comments, in the README, and in the names of the two design entries that said "him". Code identifiers (the `his` stone mark, the `.him` class) are left alone because the player never sees them. Cache-bust stamp moves 3 -> 4 so her phone fetches the new text.

properties.name: nymath's design moves from the local store to flo2.io, keeping its id
properties.rationale: @ajs, 2026-10-01: "can you put the design of /home/ajs7/project/nymath on flo2.io?" Done the way flo2's own design moved on 2026-09-28 (flo2 chg:flo2s-design-moves-to-flo2-io-2026-09-28), under the settled rules that a repo's design moves to a server once, by import, keeping its identity, and that an export is a copy. Written BEFORE the final export so the record of the move travels with the design.

properties.name: Ember goes alone, and she tells him her name
properties.rationale: The quest is the design's first answer to a hole open since genesis: nothing in it could tell whether she had understood anything. A pupil performing unaided is the oldest answer there is, and it costs nothing extra because what he can do out there is just the lesson content read backwards. The naming settles the privacy question the public repository created — typed in rather than written in, so the source carries no child's name. Not chosen, and kept on record: quests as dressing, riddles at gates, a world map. The riddle shape was the one that had to be refused outright, because a riddle answered by typing is a quiz in a costume and the design forbids anything guessable.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary: Two ideas were promoted out of brainstorming on the owner's word and built the same day. She now types her name on first run — kept on her phone, never in the public repository — and Ember uses it. And when she has taught him all five Grade 3 lessons, he stores forty-two fish for winter without her over eighteen beats, reaching for each lesson by name while the shelf builds itself under his narration. The nest gained the ability to perform as well as be tapped, and the rim now runs round whatever was actually built rather than round the lattice.

properties.name: Ambience
properties.purpose: Wind, a low cave drone and occasional soft bells, synthesized in the browser with the Web Audio API rather than downloaded — the same route musicjug took, so the site carries no audio files. Also the small sounds of laying a stone and of Ember understanding something. Muteable, and the mute is remembered.

properties.name: Ember
properties.purpose: The drake herself: drawn as inline SVG so she scales on any phone and costs no image download, with moods (curious, muddled, thinking, delighted, sleepy) and a speech line. Ember is the one who gets things wrong, so a mistake belongs to Ember rather than to the player.

properties.name: Lesson content, keyed by standard
properties.purpose: The grade's lessons as plain data: each one names the NY standard codes it serves, what Ember gets wrong, what the player is asked to show her, the rule that decides whether the player has, and what Ember says when she gets it. Adding a grade means adding one of these files. No lesson contains code.

properties.name: The lesson engine
properties.purpose: Walks her through a lesson's stages: sets up Ember's wrong attempt, watches what she builds, runs the lesson's named check rule, and shows the reveal — the maths sentence that was true all along. The check rules live here so that content stays data; adding a rule is the only reason this file grows.

properties.name: What she has taught Ember
properties.purpose: Her progress in the phone's own storage — which lessons Ember has learned, where she is, whether sound is muted. No account, no server, nothing leaves the phone.

properties.name: The page
properties.purpose: The single page she opens: layout for a phone held upright, the top bar, and the boot that wakes Ember on her first tap (which is also what browsers require before any sound may play).

properties.name: The teaching surface
properties.purpose: The thing she actually touches to show Ember something — for Grade 3 the nest: a lattice she taps to lay stones, and slots around the outside for the twig rim. It knows nothing about any particular lesson; it renders a state, reports taps, and a lesson's check rule decides whether what she built is right. Every later grade's picture (fraction bars, protractor, coordinate map) is meant to plug in here rather than fork the game.

properties.description: The owner of this design and the person building it — the player's dad. Also built musicjug/jugbeats, the GitHub Pages game this one is modeled on. Everything here is his word unless marked otherwise.
properties.name: Anthony (ajs7)

properties.description: The agent that seeded this design at genesis on 2026-09-21 and does the building. Anything it inferred rather than heard is marked INFERRED in the node text.
properties.name: Claude Code (Opus 5)

properties.decision: Of the four things this could optimize for — she keeps coming back, she actually understands it, every NYS standard is covered, easy to extend — the owner chose SHE ACTUALLY UNDERSTANDS IT. The pictures do the teaching; no guess-and-check that rewards trial over reasoning; speed is never the win condition. Completeness against the PDF and raw pull are both subordinate to that.
properties.name: This game is built so she understands it, not so she scores well
properties.rationale: Owner's word, 2026-09-21, asked directly with the trade-off visible. The structural consequence — quality_target = maintainability — is CLAUDE'S INFERENCE, not the owner's: if the goal is that she understands, then the explanation, the picture and the problems for a given standard will be reworked repeatedly as we find out what she does not get, so the things that change together must live together. Overturn it if that reasoning is wrong.

properties.decision: Ember is female. Everything the player can read — the door, the buttons, Ember's titles, the page description — says she/her of Ember, and so do the code comments, the README and this design's current-state text.
properties.name: Ember is a girl
properties.no_relation_note: Searched for Ember's sex or pronoun anywhere in the design: nothing had ever decided it, the "he" was a default nobody chose. The creature decision (Ember the drake) and the teaching decision describe Ember but say nothing that depends on sex, so neither is contradicted.
properties.rationale: Owner's word, 2026-09-30: "can we make Ember a girl?" — the same afternoon he had already written to the player "You'll have to feed her well ... She's just a baby dragon right now". Until then the game, the README and this design all called Ember "he", and the player herself wrote "walk him ... feed him ... fly with him" that day, so she will see the switch. A HAZARD FOR ANYONE WRITING ABOUT THIS DESIGN FROM HERE ON: the player is "she" too. On screen it is harmless, because the game addresses her as "you"; in comments and design prose, name Ember wherever both appear in one sentence rather than writing "she taught her". Decision records written before this date still say "he" and are left as written, because they record what was said at the time.

properties.decision: The creature is Ember, a drake, with one arc across three grades — the SAME creature gaining powers, never replaced. Grade 3: a ground-bound hatchling whose nest is built from stones laid in arrays (area, perimeter, multiplication within 100) and who eats in equal shares (unit fractions on a number line). Grade 4: wings come in — they must mirror to work, which makes line symmetry the creature itself, and its glide angle is a real measured angle. Its HOARD begins, and the hoard IS the place value system: 10 copper = 1 silver, 10 silver = 1 gold, 10 gold = 1 crown, up to 1,000,000. Splitting the hoard fairly is equivalent fractions. Grade 5: it flies — the cave chamber that holds the hoard is volume, the map it flies is the coordinate plane, and gem weights are decimals to hundredths. The earned currency is the hoard.
properties.name: The pet is Ember, a drake, and its hoard is the place value system
properties.rationale: Owner chose it over a moth and a build-it-yourself rover, 2026-09-21. Three reasons it won. (1) The hoard is the best model available for NY-4.NBT.1 — "a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right" is not a metaphor for a pile of coins that trade ten-for-one, it is literally the same statement, and Grade 4 place value is the largest block of content in the owner's primary grade. (2) A drake is warm without being young; the moth's metamorphosis, though a better natural arc, is a first-grade science topic and risked reading as babyish to a fourth grader. (3) Ground -> wings -> flight maps onto the standards' own progression of flat area, then angle and symmetry, then volume and coordinates, so the creature's growth and the mathematics advance together rather than one decorating the other.

properties.decision: The Grade 3 review comes first and unlocks the Grade 4 content. It is not mixed in per-topic, not an optional side area, and not adaptively routed by a placement check.
properties.name: Grade 3 is a gate she clears before Grade 4 opens
properties.rationale: Owner's word, 2026-09-21, chosen with the downside stated: it is a wall of review before she reaches anything new. OPEN RISK, not yet answered: a gate she cannot clear is a game she stops playing, which directly threatens dec:built-for-understanding. How long the Grade 3 gate is, and what "cleared" means, are undecided.

properties.chose: Candidate (b) won: the SAME creature gains powers, it is never replaced. Choosing Ember settled it — a drake that hatches, grows wings, then flies is one continuous creature, so the "new pet at each grade" option is off the table. The reason (a) lost is the one recorded when the idea was captured: replacing the pet discards the attachment that was the whole point of having one, at exactly the moment she earns the reward. Superseded rather than accepted because dec:ember-the-drake now carries the full answer.
properties.decision: IDEA, NOT SETTLED. Crossing a grade boundary is marked on the pet itself. Two candidates the owner floated: (a) she gets a NEW pet at each grade, or (b) her existing pet GAINS POWERS — his example was that it starts to fly. A third that follows from the same thought but nobody has said: some mix, where the pet evolves rather than being replaced.
properties.name: Crossing a grade changes the pet — new creature, or powers like flight
properties.rationale: Owner's words, 2026-09-21, prefaced with "Maybe" — recorded as a live idea rather than as intent, and deliberately left proposed. It matters more than it looks: it is the first thing said about what the creature actually IS, which dec:pet-you-grow left open, and it implies the pet has a visible arc spanning three grades rather than a single fixed form. The two candidates are NOT equivalent — (b) keeps everything she has built and makes the grade jump feel like her own growth, while (a) starts her over and risks discarding the attachment that was the whole reason for a pet. That argues for (b), but it is the owner's call and he has not made it.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. The owner wants quests involving maths puzzles and riddles. Four shapes, which are not variations of one idea — they are different games. (a) QUESTS AS DRESSING: each existing lesson gets a destination and a reason. "The nest must be finished before the frost." Nearly free, since it is words around what is already built, and it adds no new mathematics. (b) QUESTS AS TRANSFER: after she has TAUGHT Ember something, a quest makes him USE it somewhere unfamiliar — the skill applied out of context, which is the hardest and most valuable thing in learning and the thing worksheets never reach. Expensive: new content and probably new interactions. (c) RIDDLES AS GATES: a raven, a troll, a locked door asks a riddle whose answer is a number. Familiar and atmospheric. (d) QUESTS AS A MAP: a world of places, each with a resident and a problem, that she and Ember travel between — the world-map shape rejected earlier in favour of the pet, reconsidered here as a LAYER OVER the pet rather than instead of it. A fifth, which nobody proposed and which falls out of the teaching frame: (e) EMBER GOES ALONE. She teaches him, then watches him attempt the quest himself, and what he can do is exactly what she managed to teach him. The quest becomes the proof.
properties.name: OPEN — do quests and riddles sit on top of the teaching, and in what shape?
properties.rationale: Owner's idea, 2026-09-21, in a /brainstorm, prompted by thinking about dragons. Recorded with its objections rather than argued down. THE ONE REAL HAZARD, and it applies to (c) hardest: a riddle whose answer you TYPE OR PICK is a quiz wearing a costume, and dec:built-for-understanding rules that out — no four-option taps, nothing that can be got right by luck. A riddle survives here only if it is ANSWERED BY BUILDING: "I have four sides, my rim is 14, and I am not a square — what am I?" is a riddle she solves on the nest lattice and cannot guess. Notably the design already contains one of these without having called it a riddle: the second stage of the rim lesson is exactly that question. SECOND OBJECTION: Grade 3 is a gate, and dec:grade3-is-a-gate already carries the risk that a long gate is a game she abandons. Quests lengthen it. If they go anywhere first, Grade 4 is the safer place. THIRD: scope. Five lessons exist; Grades 4 and 5 are unwritten. Quests are a second content axis crossing the first, and two axes multiply. WHAT ARGUES FOR (e) AND (b): they are the only shapes that add a new kind of understanding rather than new scenery, and (e) costs least of the two because Ember attempting a task he was taught reuses the lesson content backwards. It is also the emotionally right ending — the teacher watching the pupil go alone.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. The owner's daughter is Ronie, and he suggested the game becomes "The Adventures of Ronie and Ember". Two separate things are tangled in that and they can be answered apart. (a) THE TITLE — what the page is called. (b) THE FRAME — whether Ronie is a NAMED CHARACTER inside the game rather than an unnamed someone doing the teaching. Today the design has no player character at all: she is a pair of hands. Naming her makes her Hiccup to Ember's Toothless, which is what the owner's own reference film is about. Options on the table: title only; title and character; character but with a name she types in herself on first run; neither.
properties.name: OPEN — is the game called The Adventures of Ronie & Ember, with Ronie in it?
properties.rationale: Owner's idea, 2026-09-21, offered inside a /brainstorm. Cheap: the title is one line of HTML, and a named character is mostly words in Ember's mouth — he can address her by name, which costs nothing and changes a great deal. What to weigh against it. (1) THE REPOSITORY IS PUBLIC. A first name alone is low risk and a great many family projects carry one, but it is the owner's call to make knowingly rather than by default, and far easier to settle now than to scrub out of a git history later. A name she types in on first run buys the same warmth with nothing committed to the repo. (2) A named character pulls towards a STORY, and dec:ember-the-drake was chosen partly because a story is the least replayable of the shapes considered. (3) It cuts the other way too: being named is what makes a quest hers rather than an errand, so this question and the quest question want answering together.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL, and it is Claude's extension of the owner's idea rather than the owner's own. The inversion: she constructs a FALSE claim herself and tries it on a creature — one convincing enough to be believed. The creature checks it and either falls for it or catches her. Nobody has asked for this; it is recorded because it follows from what the owner said about his own game, where the delight eventually flips and the child starts trying it on the parent.
properties.name: OPEN — does she get to build the lie, and trick the creature back?
properties.rationale: Claude's idea, 2026-09-21, extending the owner's. WHY IT IS WORTH MORE THAN IT LOOKS: to build a lie that will be believed you have to understand the truth completely and then depart from it deliberately and by a controlled amount. "Make 6 x 7 wrong, but only just" requires knowing that it is 42 AND knowing what a plausible near-miss looks like — 43, or 36 from the neighbouring fact, rather than 900. That is a step beyond refutation, and it cannot be done by guessing at all. The error she builds also SHOWS what she thinks a typical mistake looks like, which is a window into her own model that nothing else in this design opens. OBJECTIONS. (1) IT ASKS A CHILD TO PRACTISE DECEIVING, and although the target is an imaginary creature in a game her father built, that is a judgement for her father and not for this design. (2) IT IS THE HARDEST THING PROPOSED SO FAR and probably belongs above Grade 3, if anywhere. (3) It shares the standing hazard with the trickster idea: a false statement she authored must not be left standing on the screen as though it were true.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. The owner's words: "would be fun if we had the math requirements loaded into reflow2 and then the kids built their own game concept around it". The idea underneath it is that the standards stop being a PDF somebody reads and become a design graph somebody BUILDS AGAINST — a spine, loaded once, that any number of games hang off. Options, not yet chosen: just Grades 3-5 for this game's own use; a whole grade band; all of PK-12; and separately whether the spine lives inside proj:nymath or as a project of its own that nymath and others point at. That last one is a real fork — a spine everything shares does not belong inside one game's design, and reflow2 has a way to make the join between two projects explicit.
properties.name: OPEN — are the math standards themselves a reusable reflow2 design that anything can be built against?
properties.rationale: Owner's idea, 2026-09-21, after using reflow2 and an agent to design this game in a day. WHY IT IS CHEAPER THAN IT SOUNDS, measured rather than guessed on 2026-09-21: the NYS PDF carries 250 unique standard codes and 340 lines labelled "Coherence", each naming a prerequisite chain — NY-PK.CC.1 to NY-K.CC.1, NY-3.OA.1 to NY-4.OA.1 to NY-5.NF.5. The state has already published the dependency graph. An import does not have to INFER what comes before what; it reads the arrows off the page. That is the expensive half of building any spine and it is already done, by the authority, in the source document. WHY THE MATCH IS STRUCTURAL AND NOT A METAPHOR: the standards are a hierarchy of domains, clusters and coded statements with declared prerequisites, and that is the shape reflow2 already holds. The coverage reporting comes with it — a game built against the spine can be ASKED which standards it actually serves, which is not a question any other tool answers. THE HONEST SIZE: loading the spine is small, days not months, and it is the one piece of this whole idea that is reusable forever whatever happens to the rest. Everything else in the owner's paragraph is much larger, and is a separate question.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Creatures along the way try to get Ronie and Ember to agree to something false — the owner's example being 2 + 2 = 5, and his own game with his daughter being "3 + 3 = 7" and waiting for "Dad, no it's not!". Shapes to choose between, which differ more than they look. (a) ROADSIDE ENCOUNTERS during a quest: a creature blocks the way with a claim, and it must be dealt with before passing. (b) A NAMED RECURRING TRICKSTER who turns up across grades and whose tricks get subtler as she gets better — an antagonist she comes to know. (c) TRICKS AIMED AT EMBER during the quest he takes alone, which finally gives her something to DO while watching, since right now her only control is "go on". (d) A TRICK LAYER over the existing lessons rather than a new place — the creature interrupts a lesson she is already in. Not decided, and (b) and (c) combine rather than compete.
properties.name: OPEN — do tricky creatures assert false arithmetic for her to refute?
properties.no_relation_note: The only near match offered was dec:idea-ronie-and-ember, which is about what she and the game are CALLED. It has already been answered (she types her name) and has no bearing on whether a creature lies to her — the overlap is that both mention Ronie, which is similarity rather than relatedness. The nodes this one genuinely touches are dec:built-for-understanding, dec:she-teaches-ember, req:ember-goes-alone and envrule:nys-next-gen-math-standards, and those relations are drawn in the review_relations call that follows.
properties.rationale: Owner's idea, 2026-09-21, from a game he actually plays with his daughter — which is the strongest evidence any mechanic in this design has, because it is already known to work on this specific child. WHY IT IS MORE THAN A JOKE. The eight Mathematical Practices printed on every grade's overview page in the NYS standards include MP.3, "Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others", and its text says mathematically proficient students "can recognize and use counterexamples" and "distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and — if there is a flaw in an argument — explain what it is". It then says, in as many words, that "Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions". That is a description of refuting a trickster on the nest. The design currently touches none of the eight practices; this would be the first, and it would arrive through the door the standard itself points at. Catching a falsehood is also a genuinely harder act than producing an answer: to notice that something is wrong you need a model to check it against, not a procedure to run. FOUR OBJECTIONS, ALL REAL. (1) TRUE OR FALSE IS A COIN FLIP — a tap that says "no" is more guessable than the four-option quiz this design already forbids, so a bare yes/no would be the worst mechanic in the game. It survives only if she must SHOW the flaw by building it, which is the teaching mechanic turned round and which MP.3 asks for anyway. (2) THE TRICKSTER MUST SOMETIMES BE RIGHT, or the game collapses into "always tap no" and she stops reading the claim. Agreeing with a true statement has to be a winning move, and that is what makes it judgement rather than reflex. (3) EMBER MUST NOT BE THE TRICKSTER. His wrongness is innocent and she is teaching him; a pet who lies to her breaks the one relationship the game is built on. The trickster is somebody else. (4) A FALSEHOOD MUST NEVER SIT UNCORRECTED ON THE SCREEN. She is nine and still forming these facts; a wrong equation left standing can be the thing she remembers. It has to be visibly destroyed the moment she refutes it, and the creature has to be legible as a liar from the first glance.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. The owner's words: "the kids built their own game concept around it. Or maybe teachers could build fun new ways to learn and then have the kids play the games... the kids are basically creating around it and can have fun learning through creation and exploration in their own lens". THREE PRODUCTS ARE TANGLED HERE AND THEY SHARE ALMOST NOTHING OPERATIONALLY. (a) TEACHERS AUTHOR, KIDS PLAY — an adult with an account, in a school, building something for their class. (b) KIDS AUTHOR FOR THEMSELVES — a child building the game they want to play. (c) KIDS AUTHOR FOR OTHER KIDS — the same, but published to classmates. Each has a different user, a different risk profile and a different order of cost.
properties.name: OPEN — who builds games against the spine: kids, teachers, or kids for other kids?
properties.rationale: Owner's idea, 2026-09-21. THE PEDAGOGY IS SOUND AND IS THE SAME BET THIS GAME ALREADY MAKES. "Learning through creation in their own lens" is constructionism, and building a thing that teaches X is close kin to the teaching mechanic the owner already chose for Ember — you cannot build the lesson without holding the idea. (c) is that effect at classroom scale and is the most potent of the three. BE HONEST ABOUT THE EVIDENCE THOUGH: studies of children building games show real gains, but often more in design and systems thinking than in the target content, and the gains depend heavily on scaffolding. It is a promising claim to TEST, not a settled result to build on. THE COSTS ARE NOT COMPARABLE, and the owner asked to be told which is larger. (a) is by a wide margin the cheapest and the most likely to be wanted, and there is a specific reason found on 2026-09-21: content/grade3.js is ALREADY the authoring format. It is data with no logic in it — the standard codes, what Ember gets wrong, the task, the rule that judges her, what he says when he gets it. A teacher authoring a lesson is writing one of those objects, and with an agent doing the formalising they would write it in English. The authoring tool for (a) may be a file and a conversation rather than a product. (b) and (c) are an order larger and the jump is not gradual: the moment a child rather than an adult is the author, this becomes a service handling under-13 users, which in the United States means COPPA, and in schools FERPA, and in New York specifically Education Law 2-d, which is among the strictest student-data laws in the country and would apply to a product built on New York's own standards. User-generated content from children also means moderation and hosting other people's code. FOUR MORE THINGS WORTH SAYING. (1) A CHILD WILL NOT WRITE REQUIREMENTS, and if any of reflow2's vocabulary reaches her the idea is dead. What made today work is that the owner held the intent and the agent did all of the formalising; that asymmetry is not a detail of the workflow, it IS the product. (2) The architecture already chosen here generalises unusually well to the legal problem: no accounts, no server, no data leaving the device, a name typed in rather than stored anywhere. That posture was adopted for a nine-year-old's privacy and happens to be the shape a compliant school product wants. (3) A teacher-built game that can PROVE it covers NY-4.NF.1 through 3 is something no other authoring tool offers, and the coverage report is the reason. (4) This whole idea is a platform, and nymath is a game for one child; recording a platform inside a game's design will confuse a later reader, so if any of this is kept it probably wants a project of its own with nymath named as its first reference implementation.

properties.decision: The game shape is a creature or place she grows: solving math earns what she needs to feed, build and expand it. The math is the engine; the creature is the reason to come back tomorrow. Chosen over a quest/world map, arcade rounds, and a story with puzzles.
properties.name: The game is a pet/base she grows with math
properties.rationale: Owner's word, 2026-09-21. It fits the understanding-first target better than arcade rounds (which reward speed) and sustains a whole school year better than a story. It also survives a phone screen, which a world map does not.

properties.chose: Accepted in full, 2026-09-21: the core loop is teaching Ember, not feeding him. The owner raised it as "maybe" and settled it on being shown that it answers both of the design's open questions — how she earns, and how we would know she understood — with a single mechanic. Feeding and the hoard stay, but they are no longer the point. Nothing was rejected in the process; this REPLACES the feeding-only loop, which was never a deliberate choice, only the shape the game had before anyone thought of a better one.
properties.decision: The core loop is not feeding a pet, it is TRAINING one. Ember attempts the mathematics himself and gets it wrong in believable, specific ways; she has to show him the right way by building the picture — laying the array, cutting the fraction bar, setting the tail angle. Progress is Ember learning, not a score going up. Feeding and the hoard remain, but they are no longer the point.
properties.name: She TEACHES Ember — the How to Train Your Dragon frame
properties.rationale: Owner's idea, 2026-09-21, offered as "maybe" and naming How to Train Your Dragon — LEFT PROPOSED, awaiting his word. Claude's assessment, which is why it is recorded prominently rather than filed as a tweak: this answers the two questions the design had open and could not answer, and it answers them with one mechanic. (1) HOW SHE EARNS: teaching cannot be guessed. A four-option tap can be got right by luck; showing Ember where the line of symmetry falls cannot. That is exactly what dec:built-for-understanding demands and what a quiz could never enforce. (2) HOW WE KNOW SHE UNDERSTOOD: she understood it if she can teach it. The protege effect is real and well-evidenced — a learner preparing to teach learns more than one preparing to be tested — and this frame gets it for free rather than bolting on an assessment. (3) A THIRD BENEFIT NOBODY ASKED FOR: a wrong answer becomes "Ember has not got it yet" instead of "you failed". For a nine-year-old being walked back through a grade she has already done, that difference is not cosmetic. (4) IT IS FAITHFUL TO THE FILM, which matters because the film is the owner's reference: Hiccup earns Toothless by UNDERSTANDING him rather than dominating him, and the tail fin he builds has set positions Hiccup must learn to fly — a cheat sheet of angles. That is NY-4.MD.5-7 and NY-4.G.1 handed over intact.

properties.name: Genesis
Preserved on write
Verify the path she takes, on the URL she opens, before saying it works
properties.statement: Before reporting anything on this project fixed or working: exercise the path the player actually takes, starting from the published URL she would open, not from a shortcut and not from the working copy. Two specific traps, both of which caught this project in one day. FIRST, DO NOT VERIFY THROUGH THE SIDE DOORS. The #l3 and #quest deep links exist for convenience and they skip the front of the game. Every screenshot taken on 2026-09-21 used one, so the quest, the carry-forward stage, the rim and the naming screen's styling were all checked and the start button was never pressed once; the game was published dead on its first screen and the owner found it. SECOND, "WORKS ON DISK" IS NOT "WORKS FOR HER". The fix for that first failure was correct, deployed, and reported as done while the owner still could not get past the button, because his browser was serving the previous main.js from cache. A check that reads the working copy cannot see that; the files have to be fetched from the live origin and run. HOW, on this machine: a cross-origin iframe CANNOT be scripted and tells you nothing — that was tried and wasted a round. Chrome with --remote-debugging-port, driven over the DevTools protocol from node (which has a built-in WebSocket), can click a real button on the real URL and report exceptions, failed requests and resulting DOM state. Fetching the deployed files into a directory and running the boot test against them is the cheaper half and catches most of it. PARTLY MECHANISED SINCE: test/boot.test.js walks the front door, and fails if any asset is missing its cache-busting stamp or if two disagree.

properties.name: NYS Next Generation Mathematics Learning Standards (2017)
properties.statement: The math content of this game must match the New York State Next Generation Mathematics Learning Standards for Grades 3 and 4. Every piece of content traces to a standard code (NY-3.* / NY-4.*), and coverage is judged against the standard's own cluster structure — not against a topic list we invented. Grade 4 whole numbers are limited to 1,000,000; Grade 4 fractions are limited to denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 100.

properties.name: NYMath — 4th grade math game
properties.objective: A browser math game on GitHub Pages that carries one 4th grader through the NYS Grade 4 standards, with a Grade 3 review first, and that she chooses to play.

properties.name: Ambient sound or music underneath it
properties.statement: The game must have ambient sound or background music — a world she is inside rather than a silent worksheet. SOURCE: stated by user, 2026-09-21, offered as "one small detail". OPEN, and Claude's note rather than the user's: on a phone over GitHub Pages, audio files are the heaviest thing the site would carry, and the owner already solved this once in musicjug by SYNTHESIZING sound in the browser with the Web Audio API instead of shipping files. That route costs no bytes and never loops audibly. Not yet decided which way. Also undecided: whether she can turn it off, which matters because a child may play in a room with other people.

properties.name: Built for one specific 4th grader
properties.statement: The player is the user's daughter, a 4th grader, playing on her own. Everything is tuned for her rather than for a class or a general audience. SOURCE: stated by user ("my daughter is now a 4th grader"). Her age (~9), reading level, what she already likes, and whether anyone else will use it are all UNKNOWN — open questions.

properties.name: Adding a grade must be adding data, not rewriting the game
properties.statement: The game now spans three grades (3, 4, 5) and the owner has said the top end is open. That makes "add a grade" a repeatable operation, so a grade's content — its standards, its explanations, its pictures, its problems — must live as data organized by standard code, separate from the game code that plays it. Adding Grade 5, or later Grade 6, should mean writing content, not restructuring the game. DERIVED AND INFERRED by Claude, not stated by the owner: it follows from the Grade 5 requirement plus the owner's understanding-first target, which implies explanations get reworked repeatedly as we learn what she does not get. It is also the concrete form of the maintainability structural target, which was itself Claude's inference — if that inference is wrong, this requirement goes with it.

properties.name: Cover the NYS Grade 4 math standards
properties.statement: The tutorial must cover the Grade 4 mathematics content in the New York State Next Generation Mathematics Learning Standards (the PDF in this folder): NY-4.OA (operations and algebraic thinking), NY-4.NBT (place value to 1,000,000 and multi-digit arithmetic), NY-4.NF (fraction equivalence, operations, decimal notation), NY-4.MD (measurement, data, angles) and NY-4.G (lines, angles, shape classification). SOURCE: stated by user ("review the requirements from the pdf file in this folder").

properties.name: The player can change Ember's clothes
properties.no_relation_note: Searched for clothes, dressing, appearance and cosmetics: the design says nothing about how Ember looks beyond the drawn hatchling and its moods. Nearest is Raising Ember, where the hoard pays for food, nest and cave; clothes could become another thing the hoard buys, but nobody has said so, and drawing that link would put an idea in the owner's mouth.
properties.source: The player (text to the owner, 2026-09-30); not yet answered by the owner
properties.statement: The player can dress Ember up — change Ember's clothes. Her own ask, 2026-09-30 ("change his clothes"). The owner's reply to her did not take it up either way, so this is recorded as hers and waits for his word.

properties.name: Ember goes alone, and what she can do is what she was taught
properties.statement: At the end of a grade, Ember faces a real problem WITHOUT the player. The player watches. Ember solves it using the things the player taught her, naming each one as she reaches for it, and the quest succeeds exactly to the extent that the player's teaching took. This is the design's proof: until now nothing in it could tell whether the player had understood anything, and a pupil performing unaided is the oldest answer there is. SOURCE: owner's word, 2026-09-21, choosing this over quests-as-dressing, riddles-at-gates and a world map. (Pronouns changed 2026-09-30 when Ember became a girl; the meaning is unchanged.)

properties.name: Once Ember flies well, Ember takes the player flying
properties.source: The player asked (text to the owner, 2026-09-30); the owner promised it in his reply to her
properties.statement: Ember learns to fly through the lessons the player teaches — not through feeding or walks — and once Ember flies well, Ember takes the player flying. She asked to "fly with him" on 2026-09-30; the owner answered: "as you progress in your lessons with her, you'll eventually get her to fly and then, once she flies well, then she can take flying" (read as "take you flying"). NOT SETTLED: where in the arc the first ride comes. Under the accepted creature arc Ember only truly flies in Grade 5, which is the grade that is there only if she reaches it.

properties.name: It must feel like a game, not a tutorial
properties.statement: The experience must read as a game rather than an outright tutorial — something she chooses to play, not a worksheet with a skin on it. SOURCE: stated by user ("Should be more of a game than an outright tutorial", "be fun").

properties.name: Hosted as a simple github.io page
properties.statement: The tutorial must be hosted as a simple GitHub Pages (github.io) site, the same way the musicjug/jugbeats project is: a public repo under the user's GitHub account, served at https://sligara7.github.io/<repo>/, which she opens with a link. SOURCE: stated by user ("as we did with /home/ajs7/project/musicjug, I'd like to just make a simple github.io page to host it for her"). The account and URL shape are INFERRED from musicjug's git remote (github.com/sligara7/jugbeats).

properties.name: Include a Grade 3 review
properties.statement: The tutorial must include a review of 3rd grade math, because the learner likely needs to shore that up before Grade 4 work. The NYS Grade 3 content is NY-3.OA (multiplication/division within 100, patterns), NY-3.NBT (place value, multi-digit arithmetic), NY-3.NF (fractions as numbers), NY-3.MD (time, volume, mass, data, area, perimeter) and NY-3.G (shapes and attributes). SOURCE: stated by user ("she probably needs to do a review of her 3rd grade math"). The mapping to those specific NYS Grade 3 domains is INFERRED from the same standards PDF.

properties.name: Grade 5 is there if she can reach it
properties.statement: If she keeps going past Grade 4, the game must carry her into 5th grade content rather than ending. Grade 5 is OPTIONAL and unbounded-upward — reached by getting there, not required of her — which is the opposite end from the Grade 3 review, which is a gate she must clear. NYS Grade 5 content is NY-5.OA (numerical expressions, patterns and relationships), NY-5.NBT (the place value system including decimals, multi-digit division, decimal operations to hundredths), NY-5.NF (adding and subtracting unlike denominators, multiplying fractions, dividing unit fractions by whole numbers and vice versa), NY-5.MD (unit conversion, data, volume) and NY-5.G (the coordinate plane, classifying 2-D figures in a hierarchy). SOURCE: stated by user, 2026-09-21 ("make it so that she can progress into 5th grade if she is able to keep going"). The mapping to those NY-5 domains is INFERRED from the same standards PDF, pp.67-78.

properties.name: The math must be interactive, not read
properties.statement: The learner must act on the math — manipulate, drag, build, answer — rather than read explanations of it. SOURCE: stated by user ("The tutorial should be interactive").

properties.name: The player looks after Ember: feeding, and walks
properties.source: The player asked (text to the owner, 2026-09-30); the owner agreed in his reply to her
properties.statement: Between lessons the player can look after Ember: feed Ember, and take Ember for walks. The player asked for both on 2026-09-30, and the owner told her the same day: "You'll have to feed her well and take her for walks and then teach her to fly. She's just a baby dragon right now". NOT SETTLED BY THIS: what looking after Ember costs or teaches. The design already says the hoard she earns pays for food (Raising Ember); walks are new, and nothing says yet whether a walk carries any mathematics or is simply time with Ember.

properties.name: She plays it on a phone
properties.statement: The target device is a phone. Every screen, every picture and every interaction must work on a small portrait touch screen with a finger — no hover, no keyboard entry, no two-handed drags, no diagram that needs pinch-zoom to read. Content is designed one idea at a time because that is all that fits. SOURCE: stated by user, 2026-09-21, chosen over tablet, laptop and all-of-them.

properties.name: Lots of pictures that explain the math
properties.statement: The math must be explained visually, with lots of pictures — arrays, area models, fraction bars, number lines, angle figures — carrying the explanation rather than decorating text. SOURCE: stated by user ("have lots of pictures explaining the math"). Which specific visual models are used is INFERRED from the NYS standards, which name equal-sized groups, arrays, area models, number lines and tape diagrams.

properties.name: She types her own name, and Ember uses it
properties.statement: On first run the player types her name, and from then on Ember addresses her by it and the game calls itself The Adventures of <her name> and Ember. Her name lives only in her phone's own storage — it is never committed to the repository, never sent anywhere, and the published source contains no child's name. SOURCE: owner's word, 2026-09-21, choosing the type-it-in option over hard-coding "Ronie" into a public repo. INFERRED, and flagged as Claude's reading rather than the owner's: that the TITLE follows the same rule as the character, so the page ships as "Ember" and becomes "The Adventures of ... and Ember" only once she has named herself. Say so if that is wrong.

properties.name: Static files only — no backend, no build, no login
properties.statement: The whole thing must run from static files served by GitHub Pages: no server, no database, no account or login, no build step required to publish. Plain HTML/CSS/JS committed to the repo, as musicjug does. INFERRED from the user's "simple github.io page" and from how musicjug is built — NOT stated outright. Needs confirmation.

{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. The owner's daughter is Ronie, and he suggested the game becomes \"The Adventures of Ronie & Ember\". Two separate things are tangled in that and they can be answered apart. (a) THE TITLE — what the page is called. (b) THE FRAME — whether Ronie is a NAMED CHARACTER inside the game rather than an unnamed someone doing the teaching. Today the design has no player character at all: she is a pair of hands. Options: title only; title and character; character but a name she types in herself on first run; neither.</decision>\n<parameter name=\"rationale\">Owner's idea, 2026-09-21, inside a /brainstorm. Cheap: the title is one line of HTML, and a named character is mostly words in Ember's dialogue — he can address her by name, which costs nothing and changes a great deal. What to weigh against it. (1) THE REPOSITORY IS PUBLIC. A first name alone is low risk and thousands of family projects carry one, but it is the owner's call to make knowingly rather than by default, and it is much easier to decide now than to scrub later from a git history. A name typed in on first run gets the same warmth with nothing committed to the repo. (2) A named character pulls toward a STORY, and dec:ember-the-drake was chosen partly because a story is the least replayable of the shapes considered. (3) It cuts the other way too: being named is what makes a quest hers rather than an errand, so this question and the quest question below should be answered together.","kind":"exploratory","name":"OPEN — is the game called The Adventures of Ronie & Ember, with Ronie in it?","status":"proposed"}

{"description":"The only check in this design that can answer the questions the automated ones cannot. Watching her play, unprompted, on her own phone. WHAT IT IS FOR, in order of how much rides on it. (1) DOES THE GRADE 3 GATE HOLD HER? dec:grade3-is-a-gate carries a recorded risk that a wall of review makes her quit before reaching anything new, and Ember was accepted partly as the thing that mitigates it. The whole teaching frame assumes she reads what he says; if she taps past his speech to get at the grid, the mistake belongs to him in theory and to nobody in practice. properties.statement: Hand-rolled a check that what is DEPLOYED and reachable at the public URL matches what the design and the working copy say — twice, two different ways. First by fetching every published file into a scratch directory and running the project's own boot test against those copies instead of the working tree. Then by launching a headless browser with a remote debugging port and driving it over the DevTools protocol from a small node script, to click a real button on the real URL and report exceptions, failed requests and the resulting page state. Written because a fix that was correct on disk, correctly deployed and correctly reported was still not what the user's browser was serving, and nothing in the loop asks that question.

properties.name: The player's first recorded wishes: walk, dress, feed and fly with Ember
properties.statement: 2026-09-30, the first words in this design from the player herself, sent to the owner by text and relayed by him: "I want to walk him and change his clothes and also feed him and fly with him". Four wishes, and all four are about caring for Ember and being with Ember; none of them mentions the lessons, the nest or the numbers. That is evidence for what draws her back (the creature, per the pet decision) and says nothing yet about whether the teaching works. Whether she had played the build before writing it is not known. She called Ember "him", which is what every screen of the game said on that date.

properties.statement: Measured 2026-09-30: docs/design/nymath.json, committed to a repository GitHub reports as PUBLIC, contains the player's first name 30 times — in the prose of several brainstorm decisions and in the id of the first-play check — first committed in 44614b5. The README and an index.html comment both state that her name "is not in this repository", and typing it in at the door was chosen partly to keep it out. That holds for the game's code (the boot test checks it) and not for the design record, which nothing checks. The first-name-only exposure is low risk and the owner may be content with it; the point is that the design believes the opposite of what is true, and the earlier decision said it should be a knowing choice. Removing it from the current export is cheap; removing it from git history means rewriting public history.

properties.description: The only check in this design that can answer the questions the automated ones cannot. Watching her play, unprompted, on her own phone. WHAT IT IS FOR, in order of how much rides on it. (1) DOES THE GRADE 3 GATE HOLD HER? dec:grade3-is-a-gate carries a recorded risk that a wall of review makes her quit before reaching anything new, and Ember was accepted partly as the thing that mitigates it. Five lessons is a guess nobody has tested. Where she slows, sighs or puts it down is the answer. (2) DOES SHE READ EMBER'S LINES OR SKIP THEM? The whole teaching frame assumes she reads what Ember says; if she taps past Ember's speech to get at the grid, the mistake belongs to Ember in theory and to nobody in practice. (3) DOES THE RAGGED NEST READ AS A PROBLEM? She should see 4, 2, 5, 1 and want to fix it without being told what equal rows are. If she needs telling, the first lesson teaches the wrong way round. (4) IS THE QUEST WATCHED OR ENDURED? She has no controls there but "go on". If she taps through without reading, the proof is not a proof. (5) THE SMALL MECHANICAL ONES: can she hit a cell with her thumb, does the ambience annoy or disappear, does she find the mute, does she come back the next day. THINGS NOT TO DO WHILE WATCHING: do not explain, do not hint, and do not rescue her from a stuck moment for at least a minute — a gate she cannot pass unaided is exactly the finding this is for, and helping her past it destroys the measurement.

properties.description: 69 checks, run with `node test/lessons.test.js`, no dependencies and no build. For every stage it asserts that the intended solution FITS the lattice the lesson gives her, that the rule accepts it, that an empty nest does not, and that no {placeholder} is left unfilled in the reveal. It also asserts Ember's ragged nest fails its own lesson (otherwise she has nothing to fix), that the free-choice lesson really accepts 3x4, 4x3 and 2x6 while rejecting a single row of 12, and that the perimeter stage accepts 2x5 and 1x6 while rejecting the 3x4 it started from. It drives the REAL nest through a DOM shim rather than a second copy of the logic, and cross-checks the shim's report against the real one first — a reimplementation would agree with itself and miss the bug worth catching, which is a lesson whose target cannot be built on the lattice it was given.
properties.findings: 69/69 passing as of 2026-09-21. It has already earned its keep once: it caught a task line of 70 characters that would have wrapped badly on a phone, which is the kind of thing nobody notices by reading. NOT COVERED, and worth saying plainly. (1) It checks that the lessons are solvable and internally consistent. It cannot tell anyone whether a nine-year-old understands fractions — that is what the first play session with the real player is for. (2) IT WAS BLIND TO THE FRONT DOOR, and that blindness shipped a broken game the same day. It never loads main.js at all, so four functions called and never defined behind the start button passed it without a murmur; the front-door walk is a separate check, added afterwards for exactly that reason.

properties.evidence: On 2026-09-21 the owner's own example of the pet gaining powers was that it starts to fly; the ride is that thought carried to the player herself.

A riddle answered by BUILDING rather than answering needs the same lattice the lessons use, so the capability already planned is what would carry riddles too — the rim lesson's second stage is already one of these without being called a riddle.

That requirement was derived on 2026-09-21 for an unrelated reason — that adding a grade should mean writing content rather than restructuring the game. It happens to have produced exactly the authoring format a teacher would need, which is why option (a) is far cheaper here than it would otherwise be.

Not yet demonstrated. There is no automated checker for "does this game cover NY-4.NF.3c" — coverage will have to be a written trace from each piece of content to its standard code, reviewed by the user.
Ember is the concrete answer to the question dec:pet-you-grow explicitly left open — what the creature IS and what the earned currency is. It has no meaning unless the game is a pet you grow.

This idea is about what happens to the pet at a grade boundary, so it is only worth anything if the game is a pet you grow. It is also the first concrete thing said about what the pet is, which that decision explicitly left open.

Shape (e), Ember attempting a quest alone, only exists because teaching is the loop — what he can do out there is exactly what she managed to teach him. Without the teaching frame a quest is just more exercises.

The two were raised in one breath and pull on each other: being named is what makes a quest hers rather than an errand, and quests are the main thing a named character would be FOR. Answering either alone risks answering it wrongly.
The whole privacy question exists only because that requirement makes the repository public. On a private host the naming question would be purely an aesthetic one.
This is that idea run backwards — there is nobody to trick and no established convention of false claims unless the trickster mechanic lands first.
The spine would be that rule turned from a citation into structure — the same document, the same authority, read in as nodes and prerequisite edges instead of quoted at.
Refuting a false claim by building the counterexample is the teaching mechanic run backwards, and reuses the same lattice. Without teaching-by-construction there is nothing to refute WITH.
There is nothing to author against until the standards exist as a design. The spine is the cheap half and this is the expensive half, and they are worth deciding in that order.
Training only means anything if there is a creature to train, and the specific mechanic — the tail fin with set angle positions — is a drake's, taken from the film the owner named.
The "maybe a new pet, maybe powers like flying" idea is this decision in its earlier, unsettled form — Ember is what that thought grew into once a creature was chosen and the powers option won.
Shape (e) was promoted to intent on 2026-09-21. The other four shapes were not chosen and stay recorded here as roads considered.
The type-it-in-herself option was promoted to intent on 2026-09-21, which answers the character question and the privacy objection at once. Hard-coding the name was not chosen.

properties.note: This capability was the open "what kind of game" placeholder, then "the pet she grows" with the creature unnamed. It is now Ember specifically, and the earned currency is the hoard.
This capability was a placeholder for "what kind of game". The owner answered on 2026-09-21: a pet/base she grows. Its description still says the question is open — it needs rewriting to match.
The warm-up's placement — before or alongside Grade 4 — was open when it was written. It is a gate that comes first.
Reaching Grade 5 is the moment Ember leaves the ground. Volume is the cave chamber, the coordinate plane is the map it flies, decimals are gem weights.
Ember's sex is what this decision settles; every line Ember says or is said about her follows from it.

This requirement exists only because of the maintainability target that decision carries — which was Claude's inference from the owner's understanding-first choice, not the owner's own word. If the owner overturns that inference, this requirement loses its reason to exist.
Dressing Ember up is a pet-shaped wish; it only makes sense because the game is a creature she raises.
The creature arc (ground, then wings, then flight) decides when Ember can fly, and therefore when the ride can come.
Flight is earned by teaching Ember, per the owner's reply to the player: 'as you progress in your lessons with her, you'll eventually get her to fly'.
Looking after a creature is what the pet shape exists for: the creature is the reason to come back tomorrow.

properties.evidence: That decision records the risk that a wall of Grade 3 review makes her quit before reaching anything new. Ember answers it: the Grade 3 stretch is not review-before-the-game, it is hatching and raising a creature that cannot fly yet, so the gate has its own reward rather than being a toll.
During the quest her only control is 'go on', which is thin. A creature trying to fool Ember while he works would give her something real to do without taking the quest away from him.

That decision demands reasoning over speed and lucky guesses but named no mechanic that could enforce it. Teaching enforces it structurally: a construction she has to build cannot be arrived at by tapping one of four options.

Shape (c), a riddle answered by typing or picking a number, can be got right by luck and would break the rule that nothing is guessable. The idea is recorded with that objection attached rather than argued down.

Quests lengthen whatever they are added to, and that decision already carries the risk that a long Grade 3 gate is a game she stops playing. Adding quests to Grade 3 first would aim straight at the recorded hazard.

A true-or-false tap is a coin flip — more guessable than the four-option quiz that decision already forbids. The idea threatens the design's central rule unless refutation is done by building, and is recorded with that objection attached.

If feeding or walks could grow Ember on their own, there would be a road to Ember's growth that needs no understanding at all. The owner's reply keeps flight tied to lessons, so the hazard is in how care gets built, not in the wish itself.
The idea was raised in the same breath as the Grade 5 requirement and exists to mark crossing into it — asking for Grade 5 progression forces the question of how the crossing is shown to her.

It would be the first thing in this design to serve one of the eight Mathematical Practices that rule prints on every grade overview — MP.3, critiquing the reasoning of others — so accepting it widens what the design must trace against the standard.
Accepting this rewrites the core loop from feeding to training — the hoard stays but stops being the point, so the capability's description and everything downstream of it changes.
